articles.title: Looking for a Christmas tree? Here’s what’s grown in Georgia, including some sustainable options.
articles.text:
Looking for a Christmas tree? Here’s what’s grown in Georgia, including some sustainable options. – WABE
Looking for a Christmas tree? Here’s what’s grown in Georgia, including some sustainable options.
Environment
Holiday
Looking for a Christmas tree? Here’s what’s grown in Georgia, including some sustainable options.
Holiday
Maya Homan
Georgia Recorder
November 27th, 2026
Cypress, pine and fir trees are for sale at Berry’s Tree Farm, a Christmas tree farm based in Covington, Georgia. (Courtesy of Chuck Berry)
The holiday season is upon us, which means that — for all who celebrate — it’s time to start looking for a Christmas tree.
Chuck Berry, the owner of Covington-based Berry’s Tree Farm and the president of the Georgia Christmas Tree Association, said most farmers sell the majority of their supply in the five days after Thanksgiving.
“It’s a pretty unique operation because it comes real quick and it also goes real quick,” he said.
Georgia has nearly 100 farmers who grow Christmas trees in-state, according to the Georgia Department of Agriculture, which publishes an annual map of Christmas tree farms across the state.
“Majority of what’s grown now in Georgia is in the cypress family,” Berry said. “But there are some farms that also offer cedar and pine. And then a lot of farms also bring in Fraser fir from North Carolina.”
Mark Czarnota, an associate professor of horticulture at the University of Georgia, said a wide variety of Christmas trees are grown in Georgia, such as Leyland cypress, Arizona cypress and red cedar trees. Those species, he said, can be grown just about anywhere around the state, and are fairly hardy and drought tolerant.
But other types of trees, including Fraser firs and white pine trees, need a significant level of elevation to be able to grow. The ones that are grown in Georgia are mostly found in the state’s northern counties.
“You need to get above 1,000 feet above sea level to really have those trees perform okay,” he said.
In recent years, Czarnota also said he has noticed an increase in people looking for more environmentally friendly ways to deck their halls for the holidays.
“I see a lot of movement towards people purchasing live plant material that they can plant in their yard when they’re done with it,” he said.
Some Georgia farmers have also found creative ways to bring a tree into their home without having to cut one down or buy an artificial one: Christmas tree rentals.
Elizabeth Beak, the owner of Joy To The Earth Tree Farm, has allowed Georgians in the Atlanta area to “foster” tree saplings for the holiday season since 2022, providing about 50 families the opportunity to have a live tree in their house without chopping one down.
Unlike other types of live Christmas trees, she said, families don’t need to put their tree in the trash after the holidays or have a yard to plant a potted tree in.
“The tree instead comes back to the farm,” she said. “It continues to grow. It provides habitat throughout the year out at the farm.”
Several families, she added, have fostered the same tree for several years in a row. This year, the farm is not offering rentals, but will instead be planting the first cohort of trees in the ground for the first time, with some trees going in the yards of their foster families and others to be planted in parks around Atlanta.
The rental program will return next year with a new set of saplings, Beak said.
The process of renting a tree and returning it to the outdoors, she added, provides benefits that go beyond just the holiday season.
“They can provide habitat for our wildlife,” she said. “They can help our soils. They can help with flooding. They can help with fresh air. They can beautify just all sorts of different things.”
Still, she said, her family has held on to their artificial tree that they purchased before starting the farm. They display it alongside a live tree each year, she said, mostly because it seems more wasteful to throw it away. If she had the choice now, she said she would prefer a tree rental.
“A lot of [artificial trees] are made far, far away in a different country, they’re using a lot of plastic and things like that,” she said. “And plus, you have to store them.”
But Czarnota, the UGA horticulture professor, said tree shoppers shouldn’t worry too much about the environmental impact of cutting down Christmas trees from a farm.
“You’ve got to remember the tree is replanted,” he said, adding that many communities have programs to turn Christmas trees into mulch to use around people’s gardens.
Because Christmas trees are an industry, buying a real tree also helps support Georgia farmers, Czarnota said.
“It’s not like you’re going through a clear cut in the forest and putting in a parking lot or a development,” he said. “Usually the land’s reused multiple times for tree plants.”

articles.title: PHOTOS: Monks gather in a show of solidarity with Buford Highway communities
articles.text:
PHOTOS: Monks gather in a show of solidarity with Buford Highway communities – WABE
PHOTOS: Monks gather in a show of solidarity with Buford Highway communities
Community
Immigration
Religion
PHOTOS: Monks gather in a show of solidarity with Buford Highway communities
Religion
Adrian Guerra
285 South
November 27th, 2026
Buddhist monks from Wat Lao Buddha Khanti of Atlanta, a Snellville based temple, joined community members for “Blessings For Buford Highway,” an event organized by We Love Buford Highway and Seeds Of Compassion, as well as other community partners. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
It’s been one year since a Snellville-based monk lost his leg in the Walk for Peace. Now, he and others are showing up for immigrant communities.
On the morning of Saturday, November 21, 11 Buddhist monks from Wat Lao Buddha Khanti of Atlanta, a Snellville based temple, joined community members for “Blessings For Buford Highway,” an event organized by We Love Buford Highway and Seeds Of Compassion, as well as other community partners.
“The last two years have been very, very difficult for our communities, particularly for Buford Highway immigrant communities,” said Lily Pabian of We Love Buford Highway, referring to ICE enforcement in the area, which is home to many immigrant businesses and families.
On Saturday, the monks were guided through Asian Square in Doraville where they started with a prayer in front of Taiwanese restaurant La Mei Zi.
The monks greeted store owners and patrons at business throughout the shopping plaza on Saturday morning. A woman greeted them in a gesture of respect, honoring their presence with a bow and sign of peace. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
Phra-Ajarnh Maha Dam Phommasan, who led the walk, lost his leg in a car accident last year in Texas as part of the national “Walk For Peace” demonstration. Saturday’s event marked one year since the incident. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
Bounlong the service-dog-in-training led the way, with Phra-Ajarnh Maha Dam Phommasan holding his leash as the monks continued their journey through Asian Square. Despite the gray skies, a crowd formed as the monks made their way into the parking lot. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
Halfway through the tour of Asian Square the monks paused and posed for photos in the parking lot. A crowd gathered around them, bearing witness to the gathering. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
Sweet Hut employees stopped what they were doing for a moment with the monks. They shared a laugh as one of the employees said, “I know who you are!” to Phra-Ajarnh Maha Dam Phommasan. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
Asian Square in Doraville is a staple in metro Atlanta’s Asian community, reflecting the immigrant history, entrepreneurship and diversity of Atlanta’s Buford Highway corridor. Regulars and visitors alike spent time outside the store fronts enjoying a smoke break and looking on as the monks pass by the final stretch of the plaza. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
The journey continued to the NCG Cinema theater in Brookhaven’s Northeast Plaza where children were welcomed to color signs in both English and Spanish. NCG Cinema provided mini bags of popcorn for everyone as people put their artistic touch on signs that read “we are better together.” (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
Monks started to chant outside of Goodwill and a father rushed over with his child, jumping up onto the ledge for a good view. They chanted a prayer and gave blessings to everyone who was in the audience. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)
The weather didn’t stop the monks from reaching the final stop in the journey – Peachtree Creek Greenway. The city of Brookhaven provided umbrellas for the last stretch, and the monks gave one last blessing and message to the audience: “No one walks alone.”
(Adrian Guerra/285 South)
After the ending prayer and speech, the monks accepted offerings provided by pedestrians as a sign of peace and respect, while some people lingered, chatting to their neighbors. This event was brought together by We Love Buford Highway, Asian Square, Northeast Plaza and the Peachtree Creek Greenway. (Adrian Guerra/285 South)

articles.title: From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
articles.text:
From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes – WABE
From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
Climate
Extreme Weather
Holiday
From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
Extreme Weather
NPR Staff
NPR
November 27th, 2026
Pedestrians shield themselves with umbrellas as they walk in the rain on Thanksgiving Day in New York, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026.
Yuki Iwamura / AP
A massive storm that stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan left almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening and disrupted holiday travel.
More than 400 flights were cancelled and more than two thousand were delayed around the country on Thursday during one of the busiest travel times of the year. Driving was also made difficult by either heavy rains or snow and ice. Some 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.
Power was partially restored early Friday, but at the peak of the outage more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and elsewhere were without electricity. Missouri also suffered blackouts after heavy snowfall.
Waves pound the Pacifica Municipal Pier after a portion collapsed during high surf and tides in Pacifica, Calif., Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. (Noah Berger/AP)
Several areas were also hit by major flooding, including Old Town Alexandria, Virginia, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, where some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, according to city authorities.
And there’s more flooding forecast. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington DC area on Friday, saying the warning was in effect until 6 pm ET.
“The unprotected area on the Southwest Waterfront at the DC Seafood Market is expected to flood,” the weather service said.
“Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth,” the statement added.
On the other side of the country, the West Coast was hit by King Tides with strong waves battering the Bay Area in recent days. King Tides happen regularly, but they have been made worse by climate change and warming oceans, as well as a particularly strong El Niño.
Part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday, roads saw some flooding and some homes along the coast have been affected.
Luke and Liam Laputka paddle their boat through floodwater caused by high tides, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, in Sausalito, Calif. (Heather Diehl/AP)
New York City’s Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain. The city can expect strong winds on Friday, the weather service said, with gusts of up to 30 miles an hour.
Iconic Macy’s parade postponed
Macy’s annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in the city has been postponed for the first time in its history and will now take place on Saturday. While it’s never been postponed before, it was cancelled altogether for several years during World War II.
Postponing it is causing major logistical problems, as there are around 11,000 participants in the parade, mostly volunteers, many of whom traveled in from out of state. But it’s not safe to put up the iconic giant balloons the parade is known for during strong winds.
There have been incidents where those balloons hurt people in past parades, most notably in 1997 when high winds caused a Cat in the Hat balloon to hit a lamp post and then strike a woman in the crowd, leaving her critically injured. Weather grounded all of the balloons for the parade only once, back in 1971.
Saturday’s parade will be Macy’s 100th. To mark the milestone there will be 100 balloons, Will Coss, the parade’s executive producer, told NPR’s Morning Edition’s host A Martinez.
“Our first parade in 1924 had live animals. But the animals unfortunately scared the children a bit more than our early parade producers anticipated,” Coss said, explaining that was when they brought in balloons.
“Each balloon has its own level of complexity so a balloon from ‘beginning to end’ can take anywhere from 4 to 6 months,” said Coss, noting they are all first hand-drawn.
Workers deflate a balloon after the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026, in New York. (Yuki Iwamura/AP)
This year there will be eight new giant balloons including Bluey, Hello Kitty and Mickey Mouse from the Sorcerer’s Apprentice.
Returning favorites include Spongebob Squarepants, Spider-Man –– and the balloon that made its debut in 1927 as the parade’s first inflated character: Felix The Cat.
Black Friday kicks off
Americans are expected to spend more money today than on any other day of the year. But, amid inflation and high gas prices, a survey of almost 8,000 adult consumers found people are cutting back on other spending in order to prioritize expenses during the holiday season.
The National Retail Federation expects some 183 million shoppers to spend over $1 trillion in November/December holiday sales. Many surveyed said the high cost of living would affect how they shopped, with some planning to buy less expensive gifts for fewer people.
The majority of Americans would be shopping online, the Federation said, with 59% planning to use AI this year to help with recommendations, brainstorming gift ideas and scanning retailer sites to find the best prices.
The organization said the top three children’s toys this year are LEGO, Hot Wheels and Barbie dolls.
Kat Lonsdorf and Alina Selyukh in Washington DC and Kate Bartlett contributed to reporting.
